content:
Back in 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of holding a "monopoly position in the smartphone market".

Over the past two years, Apple has repeatedly publicly expressed opposition to the lawsuit. According to the latest report from Bloomberg, the Department of Justice and Apple are currently in negotiations over a settlement.

Bloomberg's report pointed out that Apple has put forward "multiple proposals" so far this year in an attempt to reach a settlement with the Department of Justice:

The report also noted that although the negotiations are still ongoing, there is no guarantee that Apple and the Department of Justice will ultimately reach an agreement.

The antitrust lawsuit filed by the Department of Justice against Apple mainly revolves around five aspects of the iPhone user experience: super apps, cloud streaming games, third-party instant messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Over the past year, Apple has made a number of substantive changes in response to the Department of Justice's concerns, including supporting the RCS messaging standard in the "Messages" app, launching a brand-new "Mini App Partner Program" in the App Store, and expanding access to the iPhone's NFC chip.

Whether these changes can satisfy the Department of Justice remains to be seen. As Bloomberg pointed out, political factors are also involved:

Apple and the Department of Justice recently submitted a joint status report on the latest progress of the case. In addition, Apple also won a document discovery dispute earlier this week, successfully preventing the Department of Justice from obtaining relevant documents from federal agencies.

9to5Mac's take

If Apple and the Department of Justice ultimately reach a settlement, it would take a major burden off John Ternus, who will take over as CEO in September.
